Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

many adjective

a large number of

also a great many, very many, many people, many things, a host of, host (a great number), a multitude of, numerous

classical

Cic. Fam. 5.17.3: multī fortissimī virī (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 343

multī, multae, multa

adjective, plural of multus; comparative plūrēs, superlative plūrimī, declension

With a second adjective Latin joins the two with et: multae et magnae contentiōnēs, many great contests (Cic., Lewis & Short). As nouns, multī are many people and multa many things.

Other words

  • permultī, permultae, permulta — very many

    declension · also used · classical · Cic. Leg. 3.31: imitātōrēs; Caes. B.C. 3.43: collēs (Lewis & Short)

  • plūrimī, plūrimae, plūrima — very many; the most

    declension · also used · classical · Lewis & Short, s.v. multus

    The superlative of multī: “very many” as well as “most”.

  • numerōsus, numerōsa, numerōsum — numerous, populous

    declension · also used · classical · Tac. Agr. 17: cīvitās numerōsissima prōvinciae tōtīus (Lewis & Short); Plin. Ep. 4.15.4: cōpiōsa et numerōsa domus (Lewis & Short)

    Post-Augustan in this sense (Tacitus, the Plinies, Martial). In Cicero and Ovid numerōsus means rhythmical, in time (Lewis & Short); classical prose says multī, or frequēns of a crowded place.

Examples

  • vērumque illud est quod dīcitur, multōs modiōs salis simul edendōs esse, ut amīcitiae mūnus explētum sit

    and the saying is true, that many bushels of salt must be eaten together before the duty of friendship is doneCic. Amic. 67

  • gallīnās multās et ōva utī habeat

    let her keep many hens, and eggsCato Agr. 143.2

See also few, a lot, too, various, more, one of.
